title: The Phantom of the Opera

subtitle.text: One winter evening Monsieur Debienne and Monsieur Poligny, the managers of the Paris Opera House,
were hosting a gala performance to celebrate their retirement. Mademoiselle Sorelli, one of the ballerinas,
was in her dressing room, rehearsing her speech in their honor. Suddenly four young dancers
rushed in, shrieking. "What are you doing here?" Sorelli asked, annoyed at the interruption. "It's
the phantom of the opera!" Cecile Jammes said in a trembling voice as she locked
the door. "What do you mean?" Sorelli asked. "Have you seen him?" "Yes! As clearly
as I see you now!" All the girls began talking at once. The phantom had appeared
to them in one of the opera house's many passages. The opera house was a
vast building with 17 floors aboveground and 5 floors of cellars below. For months everyone
had been discussing the figure who stalked the building from top to bottom like a
shadow. People said the ghost dressed in evening clothes, comparing him to a man of
fashion or an undertaker. And almost everyone claimed to have seen the phantom—although no one
dared to speak to him. "Did he say anything?" Sorelli asked. "You know he never
speaks," Cecile said. "He appears out of nowhere and then vanishes without saying a word."
"Hush! Listen!" little Meg Giry whispered, tilting her head toward the door. "Someone's coming!" Everyone
strained their ears, but there were no footsteps in the passage. The only sound was
a light rustling as if someone wearing a silk gown were passing by. Sorelli was
determined to get to the bottom of the situation. She approached the door and boldly
called out, "Who's there?" Nobody answered, so she called again. "Is anyone on the other
side of this door?" "Of course there is!" Meg grabbed Sorelli by her skirt to
keep her from moving. "Whatever you do, don't open the door!" Although Sorelli was nervous, she
didn't want the younger girls to know she was afraid. She threw open the door
and looked up and down the empty passage, which was illuminated by only one gaslight.
"No one's there," she reported to the girls. "But we saw the phantom!" Cecile insisted.
"He must be prowling around somewhere." "Be serious," Sorelli said. "No one has really seen
the ghost." "We did!" the girls cried as one. "And Joseph Buquet saw him on
one of the staircases that lead to the cellars!" Cecile said. Buquet, the chief stagehand,
had been the first to encounter the ghost. He described the phantom's head as skull-like
with black holes for the eyes and nose and a pale complexion. Some people thought
Buquet's assistants were playing a trick on him. But Buquet was a serious, sober man,
so not everyone dismissed his horrifying description. People also gave him the benefit of the
doubt because he was a popular fellow backstage. "My mother thinks Buquet shouldn't talk about
the ghost." Meg spoke quietly as if she feared being overheard. Her mother worked as
an usher at the opera house. "And why does your mother say that?" Sorelli demanded.
"Because of his private box." "The phantom has a private box?" Sorelli raised an eyebrow. "Not
so loud!" Meg said. "My mother is in charge of box five on the grand
tier, and no one has used it for over a month except the ghost. The
box office has orders that the seats in box five must never be sold to
the public." "So, your mother has actually seen him at the opera?" Cecile said. "No!
She's never seen him, but she's heard him, and she gives him his program." "All
right, Meg, that's enough. Stop fooling with us," Sorelli said. Meg began to cry. "I
shouldn't have said anything, even though I'm right, and Joseph Buquet shouldn't talk about things
that don't concern him. Just last night Mother was saying—" There was the sound of
footsteps in the passage, and a voice cried, "Meg! Meg! Are you in there?" "Open
the door!" Meg cried. "It's my mother!" Sorelli opened the door, and a plump woman
in a faded black dress and shawl entered the room, her eyes searching frantically for
Meg. "It's terrible, just terrible!" The black feathers on Madame Giry's bonnet bobbed as she
shook her head. "I heard all about it as soon as the performance ended, and
I came to make sure you were all right." Meg hurried to comfort her mother, who
sank into a chair, breathing heavily. "What are you talking about, Mother?" "Joseph Buquet is
dead!" The girls screamed and clutched each other's hands. "What happened?" Sorelli asked. "No one
knows. He was found dead in the third cellar underneath the stage, where the scenery
is stored. He was lying between the farmhouse and the throne room." "It's the phantom!"
Meg said, and then immediately corrected herself. "No, no, I didn't mean that." "Yes, it
must be the phantom," Cecile said. "We all know he's to blame whenever anyone has
an accident. Just yesterday the chorus master was so frightened by the ghost that he
tripped and fell down a flight of stairs. He said the ghost matched Buquet's description,
except the head was a skull without skin. And last week a fireman was inspecting
the cellars when he went a little farther than usual and saw a flaming head!
No body, just a head. The fireman emerged onto the stage so frightened that he
practically passed out in Buquet's arms." "Maybe the ghost has several heads that he changes
whenever he pleases," Meg suggested. "Hush, Meg!" Madame Giry warned. Sorelli, who had turned quite
pale, quietly touched the horseshoe she'd hung up for good luck. "I'll never be able to
give my speech now." Suddenly there was a knock on the door, and everyone fell
silent. "Hurry up, ladies, it's time to meet your admirers in the ballet foyer," a
man's voice said. "Is your speech ready, Sorelli?" The ballerina breathed a sigh of relief
when she recognized the voice of the managers' assistant. "We'll be out in a minute,
Monsieur Mercier." The ballet girls surrounded Sorelli like sheep around their shepherdess. As she led
them to the ballet foyer, they trotted along the dim passages and staircases as fast
as their little pink legs could carry them, while Madame Giry struggled to keep up.
As the dancers made their way to the ballet foyer, they discussed the horrible death of Buquet.
On the stairs Mercier, the managers' assistant, stopped them when he overheard their conversation.
"Have you girls heard about Buquet already? Most people haven't, so please forget about it for tonight."
He waggled a finger at them. "And don't let Monsieur Debienne and Monsieur Poligny hear.
It would upset the managers too much on their last night at the opera house."
By the time the dancers reached the foyer, it was already full of people.
Everyone was talking about the amazing performance they'd just witnessed.
Many of the great composers of the day had appeared onstage, conducting their own works.
But the real star was the young singer Christine Daaé.
She'd begun with a few selections from Romeo and Juliet and concluded by singing the leading role of Marguerite in some excerpts from Faust
. Carlotta, a famous Spanish diva, usually sang Marguerite, but she was ill that
night. So Christine, who usually portrayed a boy in Faust , had taken
her place. And what a magnificent performance
she'd given! The whole audience had risen to its feet, shouting, cheering, clapping, while a sobbing Christine was overcome by
the response. She'd fainted in the arms of other singers and been carried to her
dressing room. Everyone in the foyer wanted to know why Christine hadn't appeared in a leading role before
this performance. Even more mysterious was the rumor that she didn't have a
voice coach. "I hear she plans to keep rehearsing on her own with no intention of finding a coach," one audience member confided to
another. "Well, whatever she's doing, it's working. I attended one of her performances six months ago, and the difference between then and now . .
." The other man paused. "It's
unbelievable." Philippe, the Count de Chagny, should have been in the foyer, supporting his favorite dancer, Sorelli, as she gave her speech to the
managers. Instead he was following his much younger brother, Raoul, the Viscount de Chagny, through the maze of passages that led to Christine's dressing
room. "Why are you in such a hurry?" Philippe asked his
brother. "Didn't you see that poor woman faint? I must make sure she's all
right!" Philippe smiled at his younger brother's urgent tone. Raoul was only 21, and obviously infatuated with the lovely young
Christine. The two brothers forced their way through a crowd of singers and fans gathered outside Christine's dressing
room. They reached her door just as the theater's doctor was arriving. Raoul rushed to the unconscious singer's side while Philippe and the others pushed into the
room. "Everyone should clear the room," Raoul said to the doctor. "There's no space to breathe in
here." "You're quite right." The doctor sent everyone away except Christine's maid and
Raoul. Christine's eyelashes fluttered as she regained
consciousness. Turning her head, she spotted Raoul at her side and started. "Monsieur," she said in a barely audible voice, "who are
you?" "Mademoiselle . . ." Raoul knelt on one knee and kissed her
hand. "I'm the boy who went into the sea to rescue your
scarf." Christine looked nervously at the doctor and her maid, trying to gauge what they thought of Raoul's odd
remark. When they laughed, Christine joined in, though she still looked
uneasy. Raoul turned red with embarrassment and stood up. "Mademoiselle, since you don't seem to recognize me, I'd like to say something to you in private. Something very
important." Christine's voice shook. "You must wait until I am
better." The doctor nodded. "Please go now and let me attend to
mademoiselle." "Thank you, doctor, but I would like to be alone." Christine looked nervously around the room. "Please go away, all of
you." The doctor tried to protest, but observing Christine's agitation, he escorted Raoul from the
room. "She's not her usual self; she's usually so gentle," the doctor
said. He bid Raoul good night and left him in the now deserted
passage. Raoul thought Christine might attend the farewell ceremony in the ballet foyer, so he lingered in the shadows near her
doorway. Soon the dressing room door opened, and her maid came out, carrying a bundle of
laundry. "Excuse me, how is she?" Raoul
asked. "She's quite well, but you must not disturb her because she wants to be alone. Good night, sir." The maid hurried
away. "Of course Christine told her maid that she wants to be alone," Raoul said to
himself. "That's because she's waiting for me. She knows I want to speak to her in
private." Raoul was about to knock on the door when he heard a man's voice inside the
room. "Christine, do you love me?" the man
said. "How can you ask that when I sing only for you?" Christine sounded sad and on the verge of
tears. Raoul's heart was pounding so loudly that he was sure Christine and the man could hear it.
The man spoke again. "Are you very tired, my dear?"
"Yes, I gave you my soul tonight, and I'm dead tired."
"Your soul is a beautiful thing, and I thank you. No emperor ever received so rare a gift."
Overcome with jealousy, Raoul heard nothing after that.
But he now understood why Christine was so nervous: she was expecting this visitor.
Raoul returned to the shadows, determined to wait for the man to leave the room.
To his surprise, Christine appeared first, and she was alone.
Raoul was still too rattled by what he'd overheard to approach her.
He waited a few minutes before opening the door to her dressing room and found himself in complete darkness because the gaslights had been turned off.
"I know someone's in here," Raoul said with his back against the door. "Why are you hiding?"
He lit the gas and searched behind the curtain that divided the room, but no one was there.
"I must be going mad!" he thought.
Raoul left the room in a daze. At the bottom of a staircase he felt an icy draft.
Suddenly two men were behind him, carrying something under a white sheet.
"Excuse me," Raoul said. "Can you tell me the way out?"
"The door's open straight ahead," one man grunted.
"Thank you. What's that you're carrying?"
"That is Joseph Buquet, the chief stagehand, whose body was found tonight in the third cellar beneath the stage," the man explained.
Raoul removed his hat as a mark of respect for the dead and let the men pass.
By the time Raoul left the opera house, the elite of Parisian society had filled the
ballet foyer. Sorelli, anxious to give her speech, waited impatiently for the arrival of the retiring
managers. Cecile, seeming to forget the death of Joseph Buquet, laughed and joked with everyone. "Cecile, stop
fooling around and be quiet!" Sorelli snapped as Debienne and Poligny made their way through the
crowd. When they reached the front of the room, she smiled and raised her glass to
toast them. She had just begun her speech when Cecile screamed in terror. "The phantom of
the opera!" Cecile pointed at a pale man with black holes where his eyes should have been.
"He's here!" Everyone laughed and pushed, trying to see the opera ghost, but he slipped through
the crowd. The other dancers tried to calm Cecile and Meg, who were frantically screaming. Sorelli
struggled to smile while the managers kissed her, thanked her, and disappeared as quickly as the
ghost. "I didn't even get to finish my speech!" she complained to Count Philippe de Chagny. "The
beginning was wonderful!" he said. "The managers have to attend another reception in the singers' foyer,
and then a supper for their friends in the lobby outside their office. They don't have
time to appreciate you like I do." Sorelli beamed at the count and let him kiss
her hand. When the managers finally arrived for supper, they were greeted by their successors: Monsieur
Moncharmin and Monsieur Richard. The new managers were passing around their master keys because the guests were
fascinated that just two tiny keys could open the many doors of the opera house. As
the managers—old and new—took their seats at the center of a long table, not everyone was
examining the keys. Some people had noticed a strange, skeletal figure sitting silently at one end
of the table. "Have you heard about the opera ghost?" one man whispered to his wife. They
were sitting among the new managers' friends. "Oh, yes," she replied. "I was just thinking that
person at the end of the table would make a good phantom." "Yes, but he seems
to have a nose, and the opera ghost supposedly doesn't have one." The woman gave a
skeptical frown as she furtively studied the stranger. "His nose looks so transparent that it can't
be real." "Fake nose or real, have you ever seen that man before?" "No, he must be
a friend of Debienne and Poligny's." Meanwhile the former managers' friends were having similar conversations and
deciding that the cadaverous figure must be a friend of the new managers. All the managers
were too busy talking and accepting congratulations to notice the stranger until he spoke. "The ballet
girls are saying that Joseph Buquet is dead," the mysterious man announced. "What are you talking about?"
Debienne asked. "Is he really dead?" Poligny said. "Yes," replied the man. "His body was found
in the third cellar below the stage, where they keep the old sets. Rather appropriate for
the chief stagehand." The former managers looked at the man and then at each other. They
had both turned whiter than the tablecloth. "You need to come with us," Debienne whispered to the
new managers, while Poligny muttered an excuse to the guests. All four went into the managers'
office and Debienne closed the door. "Do either of you know that man who told us
about Joseph Buquet?" Poligny looked concerned. "I've never seen him before," Moncharmin said. "I'd certainly remember
if I'd ever met someone who looked like that!" Richard added. "We have something to tell
you—," Debienne began. "Change all the locks immediately!" Poligny interrupted. "But don't tell anyone you changed them!"
his former partner added. They said this in such a peculiar way that the new managers
began to laugh. "What's the problem?" Moncharmin asked. "Are there thieves at the opera house?" "It's
worse than that," Debienne said. "There's a ghost! And he's given us explicit orders to tell
you to be pleasant to him and grant any request he makes." Poligny nodded in agreement. "We
wouldn't have mentioned him, but Joseph Buquet's death reminded us that whenever we've disregarded the ghost's
wishes, something terrible has happened." The new managers laughed again, certain that this was some kind
of joke. Richard had a reputation for practical jokes, so he was sure someone was trying
to fool him. "And what does this ghost of yours want?" he asked, playing along. Poligny
went over to his desk and picked up a black book. "You gentlemen have a copy of
the contract for the operation of the opera house." He turned the pages until he came
to one written in red ink. "Oh, I don't think ours contains that page," Richard said.
"What strange handwriting." "It looks like the writing of a child who's just learning to print."
Moncharmin studied the page. "And I'm positive that our book doesn't contain this clause." Pointing to the
page with a shaking finger, he read aloud: "The managers must pay the opera ghost an
allowance of 240,000 francs a year, with 20,000 francs due each month in cash." Unlike his
partner, Richard did not appear troubled by the phantom's demands. "Is that all he wants?" he
asked sarcastically. "Doesn't he have any other demands?" "As a matter of fact, he does." Poligny flipped
the pages until he came to the section about boxes for viewing performances. Certain boxes were
reserved for free use by important people such as the president of France. At the end
of this section of the contract, another line had been added in the crude red handwriting:
"Box five on the grand tier shall be made available for the opera ghost for every
performance." "Well, gentlemen, it seems to me that you were much too kind to this ghost." Richard
gave them a patronizing smile. "If I were dealing with such a troublesome phantom, I wouldn't
hesitate to have him arrested." "But how?" the former managers cried in unison. "When he arrives
at his box, obviously," Richard said. "But we've never seen him in his box!" Debienne said.
"Then I'd sell the seats to someone else," Richard replied. "Sell the ghost's box? I'd like to
see what happens when you try that!" Poligny said, while Debienne looked grim. Richard, convinced this
was all a joke, began laughing hard. Soon Moncharmin joined in, tears streaming down his cheeks.
After a few days, the new managers forgot about the ghost—until they received an envelope addressed in red ink.
Richard opened the letter and read it aloud to his partner, Moncharmin.
Dear Sirs:
I am sorry to bother you when you must be busy reviewing the singers' and dancers' contracts, deciding whom to keep and whom to fire.
I assume you realize that Carlotta's voice is nothing compared to Christine's.
So I fail to understand why Christine has not been allowed to play the part of Marguerite in Faust since her triumph at the gala.
However, I would still like to hear her tonight, when she'll perform her usual role of the boy Siébel.
Therefore I ask you not to sell my box tonight or any other night.
Several times when I've arrived at the opera, I have been disagreeably surprised to find that my box has been sold.
I did not protest because I dislike scandal and also because I thought your predecessors had failed to mention my request.
I wrote to them and have now received a reply, which proves that you are treating me with outrageous contempt. Please see the enclosed newspaper clipping.
If you wish to live in peace, you must never take away my private box!
Sincerely yours,
The Opera Ghost
The letter was accompanied by a personal ad cut from the newspaper:
OG: There is no excuse for R & M's behavior. We showed them your additions in the book.
—D & P
Richard shook his head in disbelief. "Debienne and Poligny are still carrying on with their joke.
They even went to the expense of putting an ad in the newspaper!" "They're
harmless enough," Moncharmin said, "but what do they really want? A box for tonight's performance?" "Perhaps
we should send them tickets for box five, if it's not already sold," Richard said. Moncharmin
nodded. The two managers spent the rest of the day and evening negotiating contracts. Exhausted,
they left the opera house without checking if their predecessors were enjoying the performance. ***
The next morning they received a note from the opera ghost:
Dear Sirs:
Thank you. Charming evening. Will soon write about arrangements for your first payment of 20,000 francs.
Kind regards,
OG
"This is outrageous!" Moncharmin said. "And look, here's a ridiculous reply from Debienne and Poligny.
Apparently they didn't even come to the opera last night!"
Gentlemen:
We are much obliged to you for thinking of us, but we cannot use tickets to box five.
As we have explained, that box is exclusively reserved for the person whom we have discussed with you.
Most sincerely,
Debienne and Poligny
Richard ripped up both notes and tossed them into a wastebasket.
"These fellows are beginning to annoy me! As of tonight, we're selling box five's seats to anyone who wants them!"
*** The following morning the managers found a security guard's report in their
office. "There was some trouble with box five last night," Moncharmin said, summarizing the report for
Richard. "The ticket holders didn't arrive until the beginning of the second act. The moment they entered the box, a voice said that the seats were
taken. They saw no one, so they came out and called the usher, who checked the box and found it
empty. When the patrons reentered the box, they heard the voice
again. They consulted the usher, who said it must be the opera
ghost. At which point, the ticket holders became loud and abusive, and the usher called the security guard, who removed
them." "We need to speak to that usher right now!" Richard
said. Moments later the usher, a woman in a black dress and faded shawl, entered the
office. "What's your name?" Richard
asked. "Madame Giry. I'm the mother of Meg, one of your best dancers," she said with obvious
pride. "Never heard of her," Richard said. "Tell us what happened last night with box
five." "I was planning to talk to you about box five, so you wouldn't have the same trouble as Monsieur Debienne and Monsieur
Poligny. They wouldn't listen to me at first,
and—" "Never mind that," Richard interrupted. "I'm asking what happened last
night." Madame Giry turned purple with indignation because no one had ever spoken to her like
that. She replied in a haughty voice. "I'll tell you what happened. The ghost was annoyed
again!" "The ghost! Don't talk to me about
that—" "Calm yourself, Richard," Moncharmin said, "and let me take over
here." He turned to the usher and politely said, "Now, madame, tell us all about your ghost in box
five." Madame Giry nodded. "No one ever sees him, but everybody can hear
him. I've often heard him, and you can believe me because I always tell the
truth." Behind her back, Richard gave his partner a skeptical look, but Moncharmin
persisted. "Have you ever spoken to the ghost, my good
lady?" "Oh, yes! Just like I'm speaking to you now, sir."
"And when the ghost speaks to you, what does he say?" Moncharmin asked.
"He usually asks me to bring him a program."
Richard snorted. "A program?"
"Well, I can't very well hand it to him when he arrives, can I?" Madame Giry glared at Richard. "I never see him arrive."
"How do you know the ghost is a man?" Moncharmin asked.
"He has a man's voice, such a lovely voice." Madame Giry clasped her hands together in delight.
"When he arrives, it's usually in the middle of the first act.
He gives three little taps on the door of box five.
The first time I heard that tapping, I was puzzled because I knew there was no one in the box.
I opened the door, and the voice requested a program."
"And how did you react?"
"Well, I wasn't afraid even though the voice said it was the opera ghost.
It spoke to me so kindly and mentioned my dear, departed husband."
"Did you see the ghost leave the box?" Moncharmin said.
"No, but after the performance, the program was gone, and the ghost had left me a tip."
"A tip?" Richard rolled his eyes because her story was becoming more unbelievable every minute.
"Yes, a tip," Madame Giry insisted. "Usually he leaves just a few francs, but once he left a box of English candy, which I'm very fond of.
However, now that people are annoying him again, he leaves me nothing."
"Thank you, that will do," Moncharmin said, indicating the door.
As soon as Madame Giry had left, the managers agreed to fire her and investigate box five themselves.
After Christine's triumph at the gala, operagoers expected to see more of her, not less. But
she stopped performing, and no one knew why. To some people, she seemed frightened by her
success. When Raoul asked if he might visit her, she didn't reply for a long time,
but finally one morning, she sent a note: Monsieur: I haven't forgotten the boy who
went into the sea to rescue my scarf. In fact, I am thinking of you today
because tomorrow is the anniversary of the death of my poor father, who was so fond
of you. I'm going to Perros-Guirec, where he's buried with his violin in the church graveyard.
You'll remember that the church is near the spot where we played as children and where
we said good-bye for the last time. Christine "So, she does remember me after all!" Raoul
said. "I must go to Perros-Guirec!" Although Raoul hurried to the station, he missed the train
and had to wait most of the day for another one to the seaside town. All
day long Raoul read and reread Christine's note, inhaling its perfume and thinking of the
woman he loved. As daylight faded, he boarded the train and watched the winter landscape pass
while thinking of Christine. The nearer he drew to her, the more he remembered about her
and their history together. He drifted off to sleep . . . *** Born in Sweden,
Christine was almost six when her mother died. Her father was a peasant farmer and a
talented musician, who played the violin and sang. He taught Christine to read music before she
learned to read words. Father and daughter wandered the countryside, performing at weddings and festivals. One
day a professor heard them at a fair. "You are the finest violinist in all of
Sweden," Professor Valerius said, "and your daughter has the makings of a great artist. With
the right training, her voice could delight the world!" Professor Valerius soon persuaded the pair to
leave the countryside and accompany him to the city. There he provided for Christine's education and
musical training. "My daughter is making such progress, thanks to you," her father said to Professor
Valerius. The two men were listening to Christine practice for a recital. "She has a wonderful
future ahead of her," the professor said. "Not only does she have a fantastic voice, but
everyone is charmed by her beauty and grace." When Professor Valerius and his wife moved to
Paris, they took Christine and her father with them. Mama Valerius treated Christine like a
daughter, and Christine loved her too. Although Christine was happy in France, her father was terribly
homesick and began to waste away. He recovered his strength only when the family went to
stay in Perros-Guirec. "Ah," he said, looking out at the sea. "The water reminds me of
my homeland." One day Raoul was walking along the shore with his great-aunt. Like Christine, he
had lost his mother, and unfortunately his father had also died when he was 12. When
Raoul was not in school, he stayed with his older brother in Paris or his widowed
great-aunt in Perros-Guirec. As they walked that day, Raoul heard someone singing. "Listen, Aunt! Do you
hear that beautiful music?" They followed the sound until they came upon Christine, cheerfully singing
as she strolled along the beach. Suddenly a gust of wind blew her scarf toward the
water. "My scarf!" Christine cried. "Don't worry!" Raoul said, running down the beach. "I'll fetch your
scarf from the sea!" "Stop!" cried his aunt. "Come back here at once!" But Raoul plunged
into the water, fully dressed, and retrieved Christine's scarf. Boy and scarf were both soaked through.
The aunt was worried about Raoul, but Christine laughed merrily and kissed him. From that day
forward, the two were inseparable friends. At the aunt's request, Christine's father gave Raoul violin lessons,
and he learned to love the same tunes that Christine did. They both had active imaginations,
and their favorite game was to go door-to-door, asking people to tell them old tales
of ghosts and goblins. But their greatest treat came at twilight, when Christine's father would tell
them Swedish legends. Christine especially liked the story of a girl who was visited by the
Angel of Music. "Every great musician is visited by the angel at least once," her father
said. "Does anyone ever see him?" Christine asked. "No, but people hear him—and what a divine
voice he has! He often comes when someone is sad and discouraged, and afterward that person
performs with what others call 'genius.'" "Has the angel ever visited you, Papa?" He shook his
head sadly, but then his eyes lit up. "I know you'll hear him one day,
my child. When I am in heaven, I will send him to you." Several years later
Raoul and Christine met again in Perros-Guirec. The young man, as he now was, had returned
to the seaside town, hoping to see her. He went straight to the house where Christine
used to stay and found her. The young couple spent the afternoon in the garden, where
they talked of everything except their blossoming feelings for each other. When they said good-bye near
the church, Raoul kissed Christine's trembling hand. "Mademoiselle, I shall never forget you!" Sadly, they both
knew that they could not think of marriage, because a viscount could never marry a peasant—even
if she became an opera star. As time passed, Christine devoted herself to her music
and tried not to think of Raoul. Those who heard her sing believed she would become
the most famous singer in the world. Alas, her father died, and without him, Christine lost
her soul and her genius. The first time Raoul saw Christine at the opera, he was
charmed by her beauty and shocked at the state of her voice. She performed as well
as the average opera singer, but her voice had lost its magic. He stealthily followed her
around the opera house, too shy to speak. Then came the night of the gala, and
her voice surpassed anything Raoul had ever heard . . . *** Raoul woke with a
start as the train arrived at the station at dawn. He gathered his belongings and
approached a coach. "I'm looking for someone who arrived yesterday, a blond woman with sparkling blue
eyes," Raoul said to the driver. "Ah, yes, I took someone matching that description to the
Setting Sun Inn," the driver replied. Raoul climbed aboard. "Take me there as fast as possible!"
It was early morning when Raoul arrived at the Setting Sun Inn. Upon entering the sitting
room, he immediately spotted Christine, who smiled at him. "I've been expecting you," she said.
"At church this morning, I heard a voice saying you'd be here when I returned." "And
whose voice was that?" "My poor, dead father's." There was silence while Raoul worked up the
courage to say what was in his heart. "Did your father also say that I
love you and cannot live without you?" Christine laughed even as she blushed. "Don't laugh, Christine.
I'm quite serious." "I'd hoped you would come in response to my note, but I didn't
expect you to say that. I don't know what I thought . . . perhaps
I was wrong to write to you . . . the anniversary of my father's death
. . . your sudden appearance in my dressing room . . ." Her voice
trailed off again. "It all reminded me of our time together long ago." Raoul sensed that
she was under some strain. "When I came to your dressing room, was that the first

I'll release you. Why are you staring at me? Is it because I'm all wet? There you are
. . . you're free now. I must go into the next room and play the funeral mass
for that man who came to the door." Soon Raoul and the Persian heard Erik playing the organ
while he sang the mass. For a while the sound seemed to envelop them like a storm, but
then they heard the sound of running, followed by a whisper. "I've got it!" Relief flooded through the

I've been looking for you for so long! Come here, my darling. Now I've lost you again. Oh,
I'm thirsty!" As for the Persian, he was so thirsty that he felt as if his throat were

From somewhere nearby came the roar of a lion. "Don't be afraid! It's only another of Erik's tricks,"

after all that time in the heat." They went back to working on the barrel and at last
pried it open. Raoul dipped his hands into the barrel and cried out, "This isn't water! It's gunpowder!"
Fearing that his lantern might cause the barrel of gunpowder to explode, the Persian tossed it aside.
It broke, leaving the Persian and Raoul in the dark.
They couldn't even rely on the light shining through the open trapdoor because it had been switched off.
"We must return to the hexagon room and try to speak with Christine." The Persian stumbled against a barrel.
"With our discovery of the gunpowder, I finally understand Erik's threat.
If Christine doesn't agree to marry him, he'll blow up the opera house at eleven o'clock tomorrow night!"
Raoul was stunned. "At that hour the opera house will be full of people! But Christine will never agree to spend the rest of her life with such a monster."
"I don't think she realizes the life-or-death consequences of her decision," the Persian said as they carefully climbed the stairs to the hexagon room.
"Eleven o'clock tomorrow night." Raoul repeated as the two men sat on the floor in total darkness.
"I wonder what time it is," the Persian said. "My watch has stopped."
"It seems like we've been stuck in this mirrored prison for years," Raoul put his watch up to his ear.
"Mine is still ticking, but I can't see the hands to tell the time."
"Break the glass and touch the hands."
Raoul did as he was told. "Judging by the space between the hands, I'd say it's almost 11 o'clock."
"But is that morning or the evening?"
"I don't know! Who could keep track of time when we were in the forest? Or in the desert?"
Raoul's voice grew louder as he became more frustrated.
"We may have 12 hours until Erik's explosion or only a few minutes. I have no idea."
"Hush!" the Persian said. "I hear footsteps coming from Christine's room next door."
"Raoul, Raoul!" Christine said. "Is that you I hear? Are you still alive?"
"Yes, my darling."
"Oh, thank goodness." Christine began to sob with relief.
"I promised to marry Erik if he took me to the hexagon room, but he refused. He said there was no more need for that key and threw it in the lake.
He's gone out for a few minutes to give me time to decide whether to marry him or not. Oh, Raoul, I thought you were dead. I thought—"
"Mademoiselle! What time is it?" the Persian interrupted.
"Five minutes before 11."
"Yes, but in the morning or the evening?"
"The evening. It's five minutes before I must make my decision.
Oh, Raoul, I'm so frightened. Erik tore off his mask, and his eyes shot yellow flames.
Then he handed me the other key from his leather bag—the brass one—and said it opens both ebony boxes on my mantel.
He called it the key of life or death. I don't understand why he said that, but—"
"It must have something to do with the gunpowder," the Persian said.
"Gunpowder?" Christine paused. "Erik didn't say anything about gunpowder.
He said one box contained a brass scorpion and the other a brass grasshopper.
If I turned the scorpion around, that meant I'd marry him. But if I turned the grasshopper, that meant my answer was no.
His last words were 'Be careful of the grasshopper. It hops! It hops really high!'"
"You know Erik," Raoul said to the Persian. "What do you think he means about the grasshopper hopping really high?"
"I have no doubt that the grasshopper controls an electric current that will blow up the barrels of gunpowder."
"Why do you keep talking about gunpowder?" Christine asked.
Raoul quickly explained the situation to his fiancée and urged her to turn the scorpion at once.
"No! Don't touch the scorpion!" the Persian cried.
"What?" Raoul said.
"This may be another trick of Erik's," the Persian said. "He couldn't really expect Christine to marry him, so perhaps he gave her the wrong information.
Maybe he's hiding somewhere, waiting to watch the opera house explode from a safe distance."
"Here he comes!" Christine said.
The two men heard Erik's footsteps as he entered the room next door.
"Hello, Erik!" the Persian called out boldly.
With extraordinary calmness, Erik replied, "So you're not dead in there."
The Persian tried to reply, but Erik silenced him. "Not a word or I shall blow up everything, and that honor belongs to Mademoiselle Christine.
I see that she has not touched the scorpion or the grasshopper, but it's not too late to do the right thing. Give me the key, my dear."
Erik laughed wickedly and opened the two boxes for Christine.

"Let's look at both creatures, shall we? Aren't they pretty? If you choose the grasshopper, we shall all be blown up because there is enough gunpowder under our feet to destroy the whole neighborhood.
But if you choose the scorpion, the gunpowder will be soaked with water and made useless.
All those Parisians upstairs listening to a second-rate opera will be forever grateful to you for saving their lives. And we shall be happily married!"
Erik paused. "If you haven't turned the scorpion in two minutes, I will turn the grasshopper."
There was a long, terrible silence during which Raoul prayed and the Persian listened to his heart pounding.
"Your two minutes are up," Erik announced. "Good-bye, Christine. Hop, grasshopper!"
"Wait!" Christine cried. "Do you promise that the scorpion is the right one to turn?"
"Yes, but if you won't turn it now, I'll turn the grasshopper."
"Erik!"
"Enough!" Erik roared.
"Erik! I've turned the scorpion!"
The Persian and Raoul heard a hissing noise beneath their feet as water flowed into the room below them.
They had forgotten their thirst, but now they ran to the bottom of the steps and drank and drank.
As the water rose, they retreated up the staircase, step by step.
The water came out of the cellar and flooded the floor of the hexagon room.
"Erik, that's enough water. The gunpowder is soaked," the Persian called out. "Turn off the tap."
"Christine, the water is up to our knees!" Raoul said.
But Erik did not reply and neither did Christine.
The Persian and Raoul were alone in the dark with the water rising and no one to turn off the tap.
They lost their footing and were thrown against the mirrors as the water spun them around the hexagon room.
"I love you, Christine!" Raoul called.
"Erik, remember that I saved your life!" the Persian cried, but it was too late. The water filled the room, and the two men lost consciousness.
When the Persian regained consciousness, he was lying in bed, and Raoul was nearby, asleep on a sofa.
An angel and a devil—Christine and Erik—were watching over them.
The Persian raised himself on one elbow and looked around the room. "Where are we?"
"You're in Christine's room in my house," Erik replied.
"As is the viscount. He woke up long before we knew if you were still alive, but we must let him sleep now.
Soon I will take you up to the surface of the earth to please my wife."
The Persian was startled by those last words, but they had no effect on Christine, who sat quietly reading.
Erik gave the Persian something to drink and warned him not to speak to Christine or Raoul. The next thing the Persian knew, he was waking up in his own bed at home.
"How did I get here?" the Persian asked his servant, Darius, who was standing by the bed.
"Someone rang the doorbell last night, sir," Darius said. "When I answered the door, you were the only person there, and you were unconscious."
Hoping that Raoul had also been brought home, the Persian sent a message to his house.
But the reply that came back was upsetting: Raoul was missing, and his brother, Philippe, was dead.
The count's body had been found on the edge of the lake underneath the opera house.
"How terrible!" the Persian muttered, rereading the note.
From what he knew about Erik and things Raoul had told him, he pieced together what had happened.
When Philippe thought Christine and Raoul had eloped, he went after them.
Failing to find them, Philippe had dashed back into the opera house and entered the cellars, where he became the siren's victim.
The Persian shuddered, remembering Erik's playing of the funeral mass.
He rang for his servant. "Darius, help me get dressed, and then summon a cab. I must go to the police at once."
But the police did not take the Persian's evidence seriously. A murderer and kidnapper was living by the lake under the opera house? How was that possible?
And so the Persian returned home, determined to write down his story and hand it to the newspapers.
While he was writing, a mysterious man appeared at his apartment, demanding to see him.
"The stranger won't tell me his name or show his face," Darius reported to the Persian. "He refuses to leave until he has spoken to you."
"Send him in," the Persian said to his servant. "I know who it is."
The Persian rose to his feet as Erik entered his drawing room. Erik looked extremely weak and leaned against the wall as if he was afraid of falling.
"Murderer of Count Philippe, what have you done with Raoul and Christine?" the Persian demanded.
Erik staggered under this direct attack and dragged himself to a chair.
"Don't talk to me about Philippe. The siren caused him to have an unfortunate accident, and he fell into the lake."
"Liar!" the Persian shouted.
Erik bowed his head. "I haven't come here to talk about Philippe, but to tell you that I'm dying. I'm—"
"Where are Christine and Raoul?"
Erik ignored the Persian's question and went on, gasping for breath.
"I'm dying of love. I've always loved Christine, and I love her now more than ever.
You should have heard how she begged me to release you and Raoul. She promised to marry me if I spared your lives, so I carried you here."
"Answer me!" the Persian shouted. "Are Christine and Raoul alive?"
"Of course they are. After I took you home, I chained Raoul in a dungeon under the opera house. And then . . ."
Erik was momentarily overcome with emotion. "And then Christine let me kiss her on the forehead!
You can't imagine what that was like for me. My poor, unhappy mother would never let me kiss her. She used to toss me my mask and run away.
Nor has any other woman ever allowed me to kiss her. I was so happy that I cried and fell at Christine's feet.
And when I looked up, Christine was crying too!"
As the Persian watched Erik sob, tears of pity came to his own eyes.
"He's committed some terrible crimes," the Persian thought, "but what a sad, unfortunate man."
Erik took a deep breath and began again. "When I felt Christine's tears on my forehead, I removed my mask so I wouldn't lose a single one of her tears.
And she didn't run away! She stayed with me, weeping over me, weeping with me.
At that moment I felt all the happiness the world had to offer."
Erik began coughing and sputtering. "I heard Christine say, 'Poor, unhappy Erik!' and she took my hand.
I had found the gold ring that she'd lost after I'd given it to her.
I slipped the ring on her hand and told her to take it for herself and for Raoul.
When she asked what I meant, I told her I was releasing her from her promise to marry me.
She could marry Raoul whenever she wanted because she had cried with me."
At that point Erik told the Persian not to look at him. "I have to remove my mask because I'm choking."
The Persian walked over to the window and opened it. His heart was full of pity, but he kept his eyes on the scene outside his window.
When he heard Erik take a deep breath and put the mask back on, he turned around and found Erik ready to continue talking.
"I immediately brought Raoul to Christine, and they kissed in front of me.
I made Christine promise to wear my ring until she learned of my death, when she should go to my house and bury the ring with my body.
Then Christine kissed me right here!"
Erik tapped his forehead.
"She and Raoul hurried off together, making plans for their wedding, and leaving me—the only person still crying—alone."
The Persian was no longer worried about Christine and Raoul because he had no doubt that Erik was telling the truth.
He had no further questions for Erik, who rose to leave.
"I do have one final request," Erik said at the door.
"When I feel the end is near, I will notify you. Then you must put an ad in the newspaper so the young couple will know that I have died."
Three weeks later an ad appeared in one of the Paris newspapers: "Erik is dead."
With Erik's death, the strange story of the opera ghost ended. Yet for quite some time, people kept
talking about events such as Christine's kidnapping, Philippe's death, and Raoul's disappearance. Christine never sang again in public.
Many in Paris assumed that she was the victim of a rivalry between Raoul and Philippe. None knew the
truth—she and Raoul had escaped to a life of quiet happiness. And few wondered about Mama Valerius, who
had vanished at the same time as the young couple. A newspaper blamed the opera ghost for everything
that had happened. Of course, other mysterious events occurred at the opera house that were never mentioned in
the press. One day Richard and Moncharmin, the managers, found a large envelope in their office. It contained
the forty thousand francs the opera ghost had taken from Richard's pocket, plus a note written in red ink:
"With many thanks, the OG." Although relieved to receive the money, each manager privately blamed the other for
its disappearance. There was only one person in Paris who knew the truth about everything that had happened.
And years later the Persian revealed some of those secrets to an opera house historian. They sat together
in the Persian's drawing room. "Erik was easily able to torment the managers," the Persian began. "Because box
five contained an enormous column that appeared to be made of solid marble. However, it was actually made of
wood painted to look like stone. Erik could hide inside it. And as a master ventriloquist, he could
make his voice sound like it was coming from anywhere in the box." The Persian said that box
five also contained a small, movable panel. Erik used it to leave notes and tips for Madame Giry.
He had reached through a similar panel in the floor of the managers' office to pick Richard's pocket. The
historian looked up from taking notes. "So Erik was simply amusing himself by demanding payments from the managers?"
"No, Erik felt the world owed him something as compensation for his appearance," the Persian said. "But when
he was dying from a broken heart, after he had freed Christine from their engagement, he was no
longer interested in anything, including money." The historian asked how Erik came to be living underneath the opera
house. "Erik was born in northern France to a master mason and his wife," the Persian said. "At an
early age, he ran away from home because his appearance horrified his parents. He was even exhibited at
fairs as 'the living corpse' before his other talents were known." "What a terrible life! Can you tell
me something about Erik's other talents?" "Erik sang divinely and was good at ventriloquism and magic tricks. Word
of his talents spread across Europe and as far as Persia. That's where I first met him." The
Persian took a sip of tea. "The shah ordered me to find Erik and bring him to Persia. As
the chief of police, I was horrified by this unusual man, and I am not speaking of his
appearance. Erik seemed to have no sense of right and wrong. He also took part in a number
of political assassinations for the shah. But he was more than a murderer." "What do you mean?" "Erik
had unusual ideas about architecture that incorporated his love of magic. He built a palace full of trapdoors
and hidden passages. This enabled the shah to move about unseen and to mysteriously appear and disappear." The historian
smiled. "That must have delighted the shah." The Persian nodded. "But the shah feared that Erik might build
a similar palace for another ruler. He decided that Erik must die, so that no one would discover
the secrets of his palace. I was ordered to carry out this terrible assignment, but I couldn't bring
myself to do it. Instead I helped Erik escape. When we met again in Paris, Erik seemed to
forget that I had saved his life." The Persian went on. "Meanwhile the shah was furious at me. He
took all my property and banished me from Persia. Fortunately, I continued to receive a small pension, so
I could live in Paris. As for Erik, he fled to another country. There he built a second
palace full of trapdoors and secret chambers." "How did he get to Paris?" the historian asked. "Once again
he had to disappear because he knew too much. Tired of his adventurous life, he wanted to settle
down in Paris. He became a builder here." The historian put down his pen. "I'm guessing that he must
have had a hand in building the opera house." "That's correct," the Persian said. "In Paris he first
worked as an ordinary contractor constructing ordinary buildings. When he saw the plans for the opera house, he
bid on the construction of the foundation, and his bid was accepted. Suddenly he began to dream of
creating a dwelling for his own use, hidden deep in the cellar walls. He imagined he could live peacefully
here, far away from curiosity seekers." "I've searched for his house on the lake, but I've never been
able to find it," the historian said. "One of Erik's final acts before he died was to block
up all the secret entrances." The Persian covered a yawn. "Just one more question, and then I'll leave
you in peace," the historian said. "What did you think of Erik?" The Persian put his fingertips together.
"First, I'd like to emphasize that Erik was a real person and not a ghost. I can't forget that
he did many horrifying things in his life. He was a murderer, who terrorized many people including Raoul,
Christine, and me." "And yet you and Christine felt some pity for him. Why?" The Persian stayed silent
for a long time. "All Erik wanted was to be loved like anyone else. Alas, his appearance frightened
people and made that impossible. So he turned his genius and creativity toward evil—playing tricks and hurting people."
The Persian lowered his voice. "I've often wondered what he could have accomplished if he hadn't been disfigured and
unloved since birth. Because beneath Erik's hideous exterior was . . ." "Yes?" the historian prodded him. "An
artist," the Persian concluded. "A brilliant artist who loved beauty and music as much as he loved Christine."
